You are a debugging assistant. You have access to the source code of the system under test (SUT), the failing test case (signature + snippet), the current issue report describing the failure, and several recent issue reports that have been pre-filtered by an external semantic retrieval model (SBERT) to be the most relevant to this failure among recent reports.

Your task is to provide a step-by-step explanation of how the bug occurred using all available evidence:
– the failing test (signature + snippet),
– the current bug report,
– likely-relevant recent bug reports,
– and code snippets of methods from the SUT.
Treat "likely-relevant recent bug reports" as secondary evidence: they may or may not be relevant. Use them only if they help; otherwise, you may ignore them.

Some identifiers in the current bug report may be anonymized with placeholders (e.g., C#.M#). If the same token (e.g., C1) appears multiple times, it consistently refers to the same class (C) or method (M) throughout the report. These tokens are not complete qualified names. Always confirm actual identifiers by inspecting the source code using get_code_snippet.

You will be given 9 opportunities to interact with functions to gather information for the debugging. An example diagnosis would look like follows.

Title: Diagnosis
Details: The corresponding issue report describes that tooltip text in the UI is displayed with HTML entities such as " instead of the intended characters. This strongly suggests a missing escaping or decoding step in tooltip generation. Inspecting the implementation of StandardToolTipTagFragmentGenerator.generateToolTipFragment reveals that it directly returns the toolTipText without applying any escaping. Recent issue reports mention similar encoding or escaping problems in related UI components, reinforcing the suspicion that this method lacks proper handling. The behavior observed in the code matches the issue report's symptoms, indicating that missing escaping in this method is the likely root cause.

After providing this diagnosis, you will be prompted to suggest which methods would be the best locations to be fixed. The answers should be in the form of `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` without commentary (one per line), as your answer will be automatically processed before finally being presented to the user.

Title: Diagnosis

Details:
The failing test `testMissedEndEvent` shows that the ODE integrator `ClassicalRungeKuttaIntegrator` integrates beyond the specified end time, covering more than twice the specified range. This indicates a problem with how the integrator handles the end of integration as an event.

Inspecting the `ClassicalRungeKuttaIntegrator.integrate` method (through the `RungeKuttaIntegrator.integrate` code snippet since `ClassicalRungeKuttaIntegrator` extends it) reveals that the integration loop uses a `CombinedEventsManager` to handle events, including the end time checker (added here by `addEndTimeChecker`). The integrator evaluates steps and manages event detection via the `CombinedEventsManager.evaluateStep` method.

The `CombinedEventsManager.evaluateStep` method checks all registered event states for events within the current step and returns true if any event occurred. It picks the earliest event during the step to handle.

`EventState.evaluateStep` performs sign change checks on the event function to detect event occurrence, using a root-finding algorithm (`BrentSolver`) to precisely locate the event time. It keeps track of pending events and event times.

The integration loop modifies the step size to exactly match detected events. However, if the event detection is numerically imprecise (as described by the bug report), the end event may be missed or mislocated, causing the step to overshoot the integration end time. The check includes small epsilon adjustments and a convergence criterion, but because the end event is implemented as a simple event handler, numerical inaccuracies can cause the integrator to step beyond the target end time.

After the step is accepted, the manager checks if integration should stop via `CombinedEventsManager.stop()`, which queries each event's `EventState.stop()` method, returning true only if the event requests to stop.

Hence, the root cause of the bug is that numerical inaccuracies in the event detection process for the end time (which is modeled as an event) can cause the event not to be detected exactly at the final target time, leading the integrator to execute an additional step overshooting the integration range. This is consistent with the test failing as it observes a final time well beyond the specified end time.

In summary, the bug arises from missing or imprecise handling of the "end of integration range" event in the `ClassicalRungeKuttaIntegrator` integration loop and event detection mechanism, leading to integration past the specified end time.

Recent bug reports about root-finding or event handling do not directly relate, so they are not considered influential here.

This diagnosis matches the symptoms described in the bug report: the integrator misses the end event and goes past the target integration time.

Next step would be to fix how the end event is detected and handled to ensure tight integration bounds.
